title: Fitting a shower enclosure to a shower tray
subtitle: Assemble and fix a framed or frameless shower enclosure to an installed tray, plumb the uprights, seal the joints, and hang the door
excerpt: How to fit a shower enclosure onto an installed shower tray. Covers assembling the frame or profiles, plumbing the uprights, sealing between the enclosure and the tray, and hanging and adjusting the door.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK shower-enclosure installation guidance from manufacturer technical sheets (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A three-sided or two-sided screen assembly of glass panels and a door, fitted to the top rim of a shower tray to form a watertight shower cubicle. Framed enclosures have aluminium or chrome rails around each panel; frameless enclosures use thicker glass (8-10 mm) with minimal hardware.

A flexible waterproof sealant with an added fungicide, used to seal the joint between the shower enclosure base track and the shower tray rim. Applied in a continuous bead and tooled smooth. Never use general-purpose silicone in a shower.

content.text: assembles onto an installed tray: upright wall profiles or channels fixed plumb to the tiled wall, a base track on the tray rim, glass panels, and a sliding or hinged door. The seal between the base track and the tray is where most shower leaks start; get it right and the enclosure will stay watertight for years.
Check the wall for services before drilling

Sweep a cable-and-pipe detector across the shower walls before drilling any fixing positions. Mark any service runs. Most tiled shower walls have pipework running close behind them; the fixing positions for the upright wall channels must clear any buried pipes.

Hold the wall channel (the vertical section that the glass panels slot into) against the tiled wall. Use a spirit level to set it perfectly plumb. Mark the fixing hole positions through the channel onto the tile. Drill through the tile with a tile drill bit (low speed, no hammer action on tiles), then switch to an SDS drill for the masonry behind. Insert wall plugs. Screw the channel to the wall. Repeat for the second upright channel. The two channels must be set square to each other.
Fit the base track and seal the tray
Dry-fit the base track on the tray rim without silicone first, to check the lengths are correct. Then remove it, apply a continuous bead of

under the base track, and press it firmly into position. Also apply silicone to the inside face of the base track where it will contact the glass and tray surface. Allow to cure for at least 24 hours before inserting the glass panels or running water.
Insert the glass and hang the door

Slot the fixed glass panels into the wall channels and base track. Fit the top horizontal rail or cross-member as specified in the enclosure instructions. Hang the sliding or hinged door onto its track or pivot fittings. Adjust the door rollers or pivot hinge to ensure the door closes cleanly against the seal strip. Apply a bead of silicone at the internal corner joints between the glass panels and between the glass and the tray.

attrs.symptom: Water leaks at the base of the enclosure after first use
attrs.cause: The silicone bead under the base track was not continuous, or the track was not pressed firmly while the silicone was wet.
attrs.fix: Remove the track, clean off the old silicone completely, and reseal with a fresh continuous bead. Leave the system unused for 24 hours.

attrs.symptom: The sliding door does not close fully and leaves a gap at the seal
attrs.cause: The wall channels are not set square to each other, or the door rollers need adjusting.
attrs.fix: Adjust the door rollers (most have an eccentric adjustment screw) until the door runs parallel to the fixed panel. For a persistent gap, check that the wall channels are truly square by measuring the diagonal of the opening.
